title: DNC plans to hold 12 debates for 2028 primary – with a new rule for Democrats who want in | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

The Democratic National Committee announced Monday it will holdtwelve debatesfor the next presidential primary starting in June — and is adding a significant new condition for candidates to participate.

Candidates will have to sign a pledge to denounce super PAC and so-called “dark money” spending in the primary, a win for progressives who have long pushed for the party to crack down on big money in politics.

The requirement adds another twist to a 2028 Democratic primary that is already expected to be crowded and competitive as the party looks to retake the White House. The DNC has already overhauled its lineup of early primary states, keeping South Carolina first but removing Iowa and adding New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia to the mix.

The DNC on Monday also named its 2028 Debate Planning Committee, led by Minyon Moore, the DNC’s senior advisor for debates, and Roger Lau, the committee’s executive director. The debate committee also includes former staff for recent presidential campaigns.

“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” DNC Chairman Ken Martin said in a statement. “The fair and transparent process and experienced leadership team we’re announcing today will keep our party united, strengthen our eventual nominee, and put Democrats in position to take back the White House.”

The first two debates will take place in June and July, and the DNC plans to hold the final debate in March 2028. Under the framework, there will be five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028.

The DNC also held 12 debates for the 2020 primary, the last time Democrats had an open nominating contest.

The DNC plans to announce more details for the 2028 primary debates, including dates, locations and media partners, in January. The DNC will also announce in January more criteria to qualify for the debates, including polling and fundraising thresholds.

The early debates may occur over two consecutive nights “in order to accommodate a potentially large field of candidates,” the DNC said. If that happens, each night’s lineup will be decided at random, with the total number of participants across both nights limited to 20 candidates.

The biggest change, though, is what the DNC is calling its Fair Campaign Practices Pledge. Under the pledge, candidates who want to join DNC debates must designate a representative who can complain to the committee about spending by a 501(c)(4) nonprofit — a type of group that does not have to disclose its donors — or a super PAC, which can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money from individuals and corporations. If the DNC agrees that the spending violates the pledge, it will ask candidates to provide a statement to the DNC denouncing the spending.

The DNC will publish a tracker of complaints — and denunciations — on its website.

The pledge is a response to longtime calls by progressives to ban super PAC spending in Democratic primaries. The DNC has acknowledged it does not have the legal authority to do that – and there is nothing that prevents a super PAC from continuing to spend after candidates denounce its spending.

“What happens when everyone denounces the spending but their aligned superpac spends anyway?” asked Rob Flaherty, deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential campaign, in apost on X.

Ammar Moussa, a spokesperson for Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a potential 2028 candidate, hinted at the longtime Democratic counterargument to restricting super PACs that individual campaigns cannot eschew big money while their opponents benefit from it.

“I love when Dems virtue signal so hard to the point they want to cost us elections,” Moussawrote on X.

But Martin, who took over as DNC chair in February 2025, has long promised to find a way to reduce the influence of big money in primaries. More than a year ago, he introduced a resolution asking the DNC to explore its options.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent, has long called for prohibiting super PAC spending in primaries. He reiterated his call in a letter to Democratic congressional leaders in August, after a super PAC associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent more than $30 million in the Democratic primary for Senate in Michigan against the eventual winner, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. AIPAC went on to support the GOP nominee, Mike Rogers.

Sanders, in anX postresponding to the news, called the pledge “excellent” and urged Democrats to implement it for House and Senate primaries too.

Sanders is among the prominent Democrats backing the new debate plan, according to an initial list of supporters provided by a DNC official. The group also includes Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, as well as Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado and former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison.

The 12 debates are all DNC-sponsored events that candidates can be disqualified from for a number of reasons. One of them is if candidates participate in an unsanctioned primary, a scenario that is most relevant in New Hampshire. The state has a law saying it must hold the nation’s first primary, and Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican,has saidhe plans to continue honoring it.

This story has been updated with additional information.
